# Decentralized Catalog

## 1\. Core idea

A provider hosts three files, separated by how often each one changes. The registry (DeDi) holds a single pointer to the provider's manifest, which is set once at onboarding.

The **manifest** rarely changes — only when the provider moves hosting or changes keys. It says who the provider is and where its index lives. The **index** changes on every publish: it lists each catalog with its status, visibility, and file URLs with digests, and it is signed. The **catalogs** are the data itself, in the same JSON schema used today.

Because the frequent churn lives entirely in the index on the provider's own host, a content update touches neither DeDi nor the manifest. This keeps load off DeDi and gives crawlers one small file to poll.

The **manifest** alone is tethered to the provider’s domain; in the DeDi mapping, it occupies the root `well-known` path, established during initial setup. Conversely, the **index** and **catalogs** remain host-agnostic, residing wherever a provider’s existing pipeline can deploy; such as an object store or a secondary origin, provided the manifest points to them. This decoupling also segments security privileges: since publishing occurs away from the domain root, the file defining identity and keys remains isolated from the frequent churn of the content update flow.

## 2\. The three files

The manifest is the stable entry point that DeDi points to:

```json
{
  "subscriberId": "bpp.techmart.com",
  "indexUrl": "https://techmart.com/beckn/index.json",
  "signingKey": "bpp.techmart.com|key-001",
  "updatedAt": "2026-01-05T00:00:00Z"
}
```

The index is updated and re-signed on every publish. Its signature lives in a companion file (`index.json`) beside it, never embedded inside it:

```json
{
  "subscriberId": "bpp.techmart.com",
  "version": 42,
  "updatedAt": "2026-07-17T09:00:00Z",
  "validUntil": "2026-07-24T09:00:00Z",
  "catalogs": [
    {
      "catalogId": "bpp.techmart.com/electronics-2026",
      "catalogType": "REGULAR",
      "status": "ACTIVE",
      "visibility": "public",
      "updatedAt": "2026-07-17T09:00:00Z",
      "schemaTypes": [
"https://schema.beckn.org/retail/schema/1.1.0/context.jsonld"
],
      "parts": [
        { "url": "https://techmart.com/beckn/electronics-2026-000.json",
          "digest": "…", "lastModified": "2026-07-17T09:00:00Z" },
        { "url": "https://techmart.com/beckn/electronics-2026-001.json",
          "digest": "…", "lastModified": "2026-06-12T11:30:00Z" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "catalogId": "bpp.techmart.com/eon-exclusive-2026",
      "catalogType": "REGULAR",
      "status": "ACTIVE",
      "visibility": { "networks": ["eon-retail"] },
      "updatedAt": "2026-07-14T08:00:00Z",
      "parts": [
        { "url": "https://techmart.com/beckn/eon-exclusive-2026.json",
          "digest": "…", "lastModified": "2026-07-14T08:00:00Z" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "catalogId": "bpp.techmart.com/electronics-2025",
      "status": "RETIRED",
      "updatedAt": "2026-01-31T00:00:00Z",
      "retiredAt": "2026-01-31T00:00:00Z"
    }
  ]
}
```

The catalog file is exactly what goes over `catalog/publish` today. The provider stops calling an API and starts saving this file:

```json
{
  "id": "bpp.techmart.com/electronics-2026",
  "descriptor": { "name": "TechMart Electronics 2026" },
  "provider": {
    "id": "bpp.techmart.com/techmart-retail",
    "descriptor": { "name": "TechMart Retail" }
  },
  "bppId": "bpp.techmart.com",
  "bppUri": "https://techmart.com/beckn",
  "isActive": true,
  "validity": { "startDate": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", "endDate": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z" },
  "resources": [
    {
      "id": "bpp.techmart.com/item-laptop-xps-15",
      "descriptor": { "name": "Dell XPS 15", "shortDesc": "15-inch developer laptop" },
      "resourceAttributes": { }
    }
  ]
}
```

A few rules hold all of this together: 

* One signature covers everything: each catalog file is fixed by its digest in the index, and the cost of signing stays constant no matter how large the catalogs grow.  
* The index `version` never decreases; a crawler that sees it go backwards treats that as a rollback or tampering and flags it, while `validUntil` bounds how long any copy may be believed.   
* Visibility is either `public` or a set of networks the provider is already registered in — the registry validates the claim, so the list cannot rot; note that this is a marker of intent, and enforcement is still an open question.   
* Extension (`extends` on a resource) resolves at crawl time,  the crawler follows and merges it, rather than a central catalog service resolving it before publish as happens today. Identifiers are namespaced by `subscriberId`, which keeps them collision-free without a central allocator.

## 3\. Publishing (provider)

The only one-time step happens at onboarding: host the manifest and register its URL on the DeDi record.

To publish, a provider saves or updates its catalog JSON files on any static host, then updates the index; essentially bumping the `version`, recomputing digests, and re-signing. That is the whole act of publishing; there is no API call. 

### Additional Considerations (needs to be detailed out):

1. Optionally, the provider sends a change signal so crawlers come sooner than their next scheduled pass. A signal only triggers a crawl i.e., content is always fetched and verified from the source.  
2. There is no pre-publish gate. A validator tool, running the same checks a crawler runs, lets a provider verify its files before publishing, and the feedback log tells it afterwards what a crawler rejected and why.

## 4\. Discovery (crawler)

A Discovery Service enumerates providers from the registry and resolves each manifest URL, fetching the manifest once and caching it. It then polls the index, verifying the signature against the registered key, checking that the `subscriberId` matches the identity whose record pointed here, and that the `version` has not regressed and `validUntil` has not passed.

The crawler fetches catalogs whose `updatedAt` in the index is newer than what it last saw. Every fetched file is checked against the signed index and against the schema; catalogs that fail either check are not indexed, and the reason is written to a feedback log the provider can read. 

The crawler also checks the provider's registration standing, drops catalogs that have not been re-verified within its staleness window, bounds what it will fetch, and refuses private-address URLs.

### Other considerations

1. How incremental updates flow \- The index's `updatedAt` fields tell a crawler *that* a catalog changed; whether it then re-reads the whole catalog or only the changed portion — and how the changed portion is expressed — is left open. Both full and incremental reads are supported in principle, with the receiver merging; the mechanism needs its own design.

## 5\. Open questions

1. How do we control access to the catalogs  
2. How incremental changes flow in to the edge Discover nodes  
3. Choosing a filesystem \- whether Git or is there any other filesystem that supports incremental diff is to be explored during implementation.  
4. Change signal and the feedback log.  
   1. Both are required, and the record currently holds two answers — "through the fabric" and "an optional, non-fabric accelerator." If either ships as fabric, it is a running service with storage and egress, and the pricing must include it, so this needs deciding before costing rather than after.  
5. The examples are illustrative rather than normative, and per-file details and update mechanics are to be explored during implementation..

Access enforcement is the second. `visibility` marks intent, but nothing stops anyone reading a public URL, and Discovery-Service-side checks do not bind consumers who read directly. The recommendation is public by default, with restricted distribution out of fabric scope.

**A note on mapping to DeDi**: These three files align one-to-one with the DeDi protocol's [self-hosted publishing model](https://github.com/nfh-trust-labs/DeDi/blob/protocol-update/README.md) directly: 

1. The **manifest** becomes the standard `/.well-known/dedi.json`;   
2. The **index** becomes one DeDi file, a registry whose records are catalog pointers (status, visibility, URLs, digests) (`beckn-catalogs.dedi.json)`  
3. The **catalogs** stay plain Beckn JSON, unchanged, covered by the digests in the index. Everything that follows reads the same under either naming
